en: 4. *Vajrabhairavatantra*: The Exposition of the Maṇḍala, the First Chapter. *Oṃ*, homage to the Blessed One, the glorious Vajrabhairava known as Mañjuśrī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Vajrabhairava, which is indeed most fierce and terrifying even to all the gods.
In that regard, first, the mantra-practitioner, having stayed in some place conducive to the mind, should accomplish all rites;
therein, the locations are described.

Standing in a cremation ground, on a riverbank, at a solitary tree, at a single linga, at a crossroads, on a mountain peak, in an empty temple, in a temple of the Mothers, in a shrine of the gods, on a battlefield, or in places such as cities, forests, and villages—the practitioner who has been consecrated in this *Mahāvajrabhairava Tantra* should, as a yogin, accomplish subjugation, attraction, killing, expulsion, inciting hatred, and paralyzing; as well as the sword, collyrium, the underworld, pills, mercury, elixirs, and treasures; and [subdue] bhūtas, vetālas, piśācas, yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, nāgas, and so forth—by means of this procedure.

At midnight, this is the procedure: first, the mantra-practitioner, having become naked with his hair disheveled and using funeral ashes, the master should, through the yoga of the buffalo-faced [deity], draw the mandala upon a cremation ground or similar site—a square with four gates, adorned with four archways, and embellished with bells, ribbons, banners, garlands, and strings of flowers. Furthermore, in all the corners and at the junctions of the gates and projections, it should be inlaid with vajras and jewels, as well as with crescent moons.

In the center of that, one should draw a circular wheel consisting of nine compartments; one should provide a single door and seal the remaining ones. In its center, one should draw a corpse: the head in the east, the hand in the south, the intestines in the west, and the foot in the north. In the eastern corner, a skull-cup; in the southern corner, a drinking vessel (*caṣaka*); in the western corner, a cloth from a cremation ground (*śmaśānakarpaṭa*); and in the northern corner, a man pierced by a trident.
One should place these symbolic marks (*cihnamudrā*) within the center of the wheel.
Now, the mudrās on the outer wheel are as follows: on the eastern panel, one should draw the kaṭṭārikā, the bhindipāla, the mallet, the churikā, the kaṇapa, the goad, and so forth;
on the southern panel, one should draw the axe, the arrow, the club, the khaṭvāṅga, the discus, and the noose;
on the western panel, one should draw the vajra, the ḍamaruka, the shield, the bow, the bell, the parasol, the banner, and so forth.

One should place the door-bolt at the front, the skull-cup in the eastern corner, and the cemetery rag in the western corner; these are the symbolic seals (*cihnamudrā*) to be established. These belong to the outer wheel (*bāhyacakra*). On the southern panel (*dakṣiṇapaṭṭikā*), one should draw the *bhindipāla*, the *churikā* (knife), the *kaṇapa*, the hook (*aṅkuśa*), and so forth. On the northern panel (*uttarapaṭṭikā*), one should draw the axe (*kuṭhāra*), the saw (*sta-re*), the wheel, the vajra-noose (*pāśa*), the shield (*kheṭaka*), the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), the triple-bannered flag (*tripatākā*), the elephant-hide, the vajra-hammer (*vajramudgara*), the spear (*kunta*), and the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*).
One should place great vetālas at the four gates and in the corners;

one should offer lamps with "great oil" if one desires supreme accomplishment. One should also place the flesh of humans, donkeys, camels, dogs, jackals, buffaloes, elephants, horses, cows, sheep, deer, pigs, and so forth.
[87] One should cause the flesh of others—such as vultures, crows, hawks, cranes, lapwings, storks, peacocks, great mantrins, great śārikas, and so forth—to be set down.
With a well-concentrated mind, one should perform the rites of food, drink, fire-offerings (*homa*), and sacrificial oblations (*bali*).
One should sprinkle the mandala, which faces in all directions, with blood.

Abiding in the yoga of the illustrious Vajrabhairava with the face of a buffalo, one should present all the food offerings (*naivedya*). Afterwards, the mantra-practitioner— having completed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), accompanied by three others as his assistants or alone, with his body anointed with Vairocana and Akṣobhya, naked and with disheveled hair— at midnight, while sounding the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) and uttering the cry "Hā hā," and being well-composed, should enter the great maṇḍala of Vajrabhairava.
Desiring success, one should offer delicious wine for drinking and flavorful food.

At the four gates and at the corners, [one should place] the great vetālas, the flesh of dogs, jackals, wolves, pigs, and so forth; the flesh of vultures, owls, hawks, falcons, great mantras (garuḍas), śārikās, and so forth. Abiding in the yoga of the lower [elements], having performed the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*), with oneself as the fourth—that is, accompanied by a very harmonious and suitable friend—one whose body is anointed with Vairocana and Akṣobhya, should thereafter contemplate the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) in the center, and above that, one should visualize the glorious Vajrabhairava with the face of a buffalo.
Standing before that [deity] in the *pratyālīḍha* posture with pride (*sāhaṅkāra*) and a one-pointed mind, one who is well-composed should recite the ten-syllable mantra.
Then, great terrors arise;
the practitioner of mantra must not be afraid of them.
If one feels fear, then those great obstacles will create a vulnerability;
when a vulnerability exists, success is not achieved. Therefore, the mantra-practitioner must not be afraid.
Then Mahāvajrabhairava becomes pleased.
Being pleased, he says, "What boon shall I grant?
The Vidyādhara should say, "Give me the sword, the underworld, and the elixir of mercury."
Indeed, it grants him any other accomplishment desired by the mind; there is no doubt in this matter.
Even if the practitioner should not achieve [the primary] accomplishment, all his minor rites will certainly succeed for him.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Instruction on the Mandala, in the *Śrīvajramahābhairavayogatantra* known as the *Śrīmañjuśrī*. Hereafter follows the accomplishment of the goal.

Facing the glorious Vajrabhairava with the face of a buffalo, the practitioner who is well-composed with pride will accomplish even the greatest fears; therefore, [the deity] says, "I give. Whether it be the elixir of mercury, another object desired by the mind, or at times all minor rites—this is the instruction on the mandala known as the glorious Mañjuśrī.
This is the second chapter, the accomplishment of all activities.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the procedure for the expansion of activities, correctly and in due order.

An enraged mantra-practitioner, established in the yoga of the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava, performs rites such as killing and eradication. First of all, the practitioner must perform the subduing [of obstacles]; how so?
Because this Yoga Tantra is primarily concerned with yoga, and because of the yoga of the deity.
At the outset, that very thing is performed.

Regarding this ritual: when one desires to accomplish it, then on a cloth from a cremation ground, using poison, blood, salt, black mustard, nimba, and dhūrtūraka juice, one should—facing south, naked, with hair disheveled, and employing the yoga of the buffalo-faced [deity]—draw this sixteen-square grid, the mandala of Mahāvajrabhairava, with the wing of a large crow as a pen.

Between two fires, having inscribed the ten-syllable mantra there with the name of the victim interlaced [with the mantra], and having written the syllable *hūṃ* within the altar and the syllable *phaṭ* in the corners; having anointed oneself with pungent oil, having placed the yantra between two skull-cups, and having set it upon three tufts of hair; having kindled a fire with wood from a funeral pyre and standing upon it with the left foot, one should recite the ten-syllable mantra.
At that very moment, the victim dies; of this there is no doubt.

I shall now explain the expansion of ritual actions, such as killing, driving away, and so forth. First, how is that rite performed? One should write this sixteen-square diagram with salt, black mustard, nimba, and dhūrttūraka juice using a stylus. Having placed eight *hūṃ* syllables in the intermediate spaces and corners, and having smeared the yantra with pungent oil, one should set it upon three wicks and ignite them; by pressing down [upon it], the target dies at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. If one wishes to afflict someone with fever, one should place that same wheel between two human bones and bury it half a cubit deep beneath a hearth; then the target is seized by fever.
The application of that very sixteen-wheel [diagram] is now described;

however, this is the distinction: having interlaced the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables, and having likewise interlaced the ten-syllable mantra together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should arrange the mantra syllables.

With the aforementioned substances, together with crow-droppings and *vairocana*, one should fix [the mixture] upon a cloth from a cremation ground and draw [the diagram] there according to the previously mentioned procedure. One should bury it in a cremation ground to kill; bury it under a solitary tree to drive away; bury it under a single *liṅga* to cause enmity; place it in the middle of water to paralyze; place it in a house to bring about peace; and by digging it up and washing it, there is liberation.

Furthermore, there is another application: having drawn the Yamamantracakra on a funeral shroud (*śmaśānakarpaṭa*) in a cemetery, at a crossroads, under a solitary tree, on an anthill, on a riverbank, at a single *liṅga*, or at a city gate—or else beneath a hearth with human bone—buried half a cubit deep, one is seized by fever. This is the application of the sixteen-fold wheel. The specific [method] is as follows: having written the mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables together with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) on a funeral shroud using the previously mentioned crow’s leavings (*kākocchiṣṭa*), one should suppress it according to the previously stated procedure; this kills. To establish peace, one should fix it. Furthermore, there is another application: having made an image of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) eight finger-breadths in size from Vairocana, vajra-water, and charcoal from a funeral pyre at a crossroads in a cemetery, and having placed the mantra in its heart, one should nail it in five places, beginning with the head, using human bone.
One should fill all the joints with sharp thorns.

Having placed [the corpse] between two skull-caps, one should fashion the form of Yama—one cubit in height, with a distorted face, a large belly, two arms, and one face—naked, with disheveled hair, holding a sword in hand, and made from the very same seven anthills. Having placed those two skull-caps upon its heart, one should bury it at midday or at midnight in a cremation ground on a site of a funeral pyre, positioning it very deep with the head facing south and the face turned downward.

Having surrounded the house with that [mudrā] while assuming the majestic form of Mahiṣamukha, one should recite the ten-syllable mantra, interlacing it with the name of the target; within three days, the target dies.
By lifting [the mudrā] and washing it off, there is liberation.
Now, therefore, the ritual application for immobilization (stambhana) is described.

Having stirred up the skin of a chuchundarī (musk-rat) with substances such as poison and having written the ten-syllable mantra upon that skin, one should take earth from the footprint of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) and fill it [with that earth] at the location of the urine.

One should bind [the victim]. Having placed the mantra of Vairocanavajrodaka in the heart, one should take a human bone, place it in five locations with a sword in hand, naked and with hair disheveled, and having placed those two skull-cups, one should bury them at midday. One should cause [the victim] to be positioned with the head to the south; having surrounded him with firm resolve through the yoga of the buffalo-faced [deity], the ten-syllable mantra [is recited] and he dies. Now, therefore, the ritual application is described: having mixed rope, donkey urine, and Vairocana together in one place, one should fill the interior of a water-clock (ghatikā).

In that regard, having placed the mechanical device (*yantra*) there and having set it upon wood from a funeral pyre, one should step upon it with the left foot and recite the ten-syllable mantra according to the *yama-yoga* method; by means of this, one paralyzes [the enemy] in a single day.
This practice is difficult to accomplish;
it must be performed by a practitioner who is exceedingly wrathful.
If not, it is not accomplished. Furthermore, there is a practice for causing mutual enmity:
having written the Yama-mantra according to the previous procedure, one should fashion a buffalo and a horse from seven types of anthill earth.
Having placed the mantra in the hearts of those two who have been established in enmity, one should set them beneath a neem tree (*nimba-vṛkṣa*).
And one should write the mantra with the blood of a buffalo and a horse.
This is the specific mantra.

One who is well-concentrated should perform [the rite] over three days; thus he causes enmity. Furthermore, if the practitioner desires to cause expulsion, he should have a camel made from seven anthills.

Behind him, having visualized a wind-mandala in the shape of a half-moon produced from the syllable *Yam*, one should place the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) upon it. Having stirred up a musk-rat skin and taken that musk-rat skin, one should mix it together with the dust from the feet and the urine of the person to be acted upon, along with donkey urine, using a cord. This application should be performed by one who is extremely enraged, using a jar, a crucible, a wooden fire-pit, and according to the previously described procedure. Having drawn the figures of a buffalo and a horse, when they are placed in a state of enmity toward each other, one should draw [the victim] between them; this causes hatred. One should visualize a camel by means of the syllable *Yam*.
Behind him, one should visualize the form of Yama with a club held in his hand; one should then imagine that [the victim], being struck by that club, is being led away facing the south.

One should draw that very wheel upon his heart, having inscribed the name of the person to be targeted (*sādhya*) interlaced according to the previously mentioned procedure, and then deposit it. In seven days, he is expelled; there is no doubt about this.
[§20] Now, there is another application.
On a Sunday, having thoroughly anointed a *mātaṅga* tree with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), one should cause it to be climbed by [the practitioner] and leave it standing right there.
Having extracted the oil from its trunk using a shell (*śuktikā*), and remaining in that very place, one takes the oil.
Having taken that oil there, one should take a rag from the blue-bannered Mahādeva and burn it with smokeless fire.
Having combined that soot with that oil, one who desires to cause [someone] to be driven away should rub it onto their sandals;
he should smear his hands and feet with it.
Even in the absence of those, he may use bathing water for the head; by that moment, he causes [the person] to be driven away.

Having visualized the victim in the form of Yama, one should strike with that club [repeatedly], facing south; by reciting the name of the victim over that very wheel for seven days, one causes them to be driven away. Now, another method: having well-anointed the body of an elephant and placed it there, one should extract oil from that body using a conch-shell; taking a cloth and burning it with the smoke of that [oil], one should smear the resulting soot upon oneself and rub it on the head—at that very moment, one is liberated. Furthermore, there is another application:
one should write [the name] on birch bark using charcoal from a funeral pyre, crow’s blood, and a bone as a pen.
Having interwoven the name of the person to be subdued within the center of a wind-mandala, one should bind it to the neck of a crow.
Having seized a crow and assumed the posture of a buffalo-faced being, one should release it while facing south;
at that very moment, it will roam the earth like a crow.

Next, another method for expulsion (*uccāṭana*) follows: having anointed [the object] with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*), one should take the dwelling of a *nimbavṛkṣa* tree inhabited by a bird of prey. Having burned that dwelling in a fire made of wood from a cemetery, one should take those ashes; when they are placed upon the head of someone, that person is expelled. Furthermore, there is another application for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*): having combined the wings of a crow and an owl with the hair of a Brāhmaṇa and a Caṇḍāla respectively, and having kindled a fire with *dhattūra* wood, one should make it smokeless. Taking the resulting ash and reciting the ten-syllable mantra over it, one should scatter the ash between a woman and a man.
At that very moment, one causes enmity.

Now, having written the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) between lines on a cloth from a cemetery using substances such as poison and so forth, and having performed the *vidarbha* repetition, one should take the hair and slough of a mongoose and a snake, mix them [with the powder], and fashion a wick. In whosever house one lights it, a mutual quarrel occurs between those two.

Furthermore, one should cause the name of the target to be released onto the neck of a crow using its own blood and a stylus made of bone. Immediately after burning the dwelling of that crow with wood from a cremation ground, its ashes effect the expulsion [of the enemy]. Moreover, one should take the wings of a crow and an owl, the hair of a Brahmin and a Caṇḍāla, and the charcoal of *dhattūra* wood from a smokeless fire; having consecrated these with the ten-syllable mantra, one should cast them upon a funeral-ground rag (*śmaśānakarpaṭa*) along with substances such as poison. Then, the hair and skin of a mongoose and a snake [should be used]. Now, if one desires to kill [an enemy], one should fashion an image out of feces and urine and smear it on top with powdered bone.

Having cut that [image] again and again, having become naked with disheveled hair, one should offer it as an oblation at midnight, facing south, in the manner of the buffalo-faced [deity] into the funeral pyre fire; by whose name this is done, he dies at that very moment.
This practice was spoken by Vajrabhairava himself.

Furthermore, one desiring to cause [an enemy] to flee should draw a sixteen-square grid on a cloth from a banner using the previously mentioned substances together with charcoal from a funeral pyre; having inscribed the name [of the target] in *vidarbha* fashion, one should place it upon a neem leaf, and thus one causes him to flee.

Now, if one wishes to paralyze [an enemy], one should draw the Yama-cakra with yellow orpiment or turmeric on a stone slab or a piece of cloth; by placing it with the name of the person [one desires], that person becomes paralyzed. Alternatively, if the practitioner wishes to bring someone under control, he should fashion an image of the target—whether a man or a woman—sixteen finger-breadths in size, using clay from an anthill mixed with saffron and *gorocanā*. Then, having inscribed the yantra on birch bark with *gorocanā* and the blood from his ring finger, he should insert it into the heart of that image.

Having worshipped the *Yamayantra* with red flowers and having placed it in the house of [the person] against whom one desires to cause a quarrel, [this practice] should be performed three times a day. [One who] desires to kill [should use] bone powder; having repeatedly cut [the target], facing south, [one should perform the rite] by means of the name. At that very moment, on a banner-cloth or a stone slab, the practitioner [should draw the diagram] of the woman [measuring] sixteen finger-breadths. Having worshipped the *Yamayantra* with red flowers and having placed it in the house of [the person] against whom [the rite is directed], facing west, one should mutter the ten-syllable mantra; within seven days one brings even Śakra under control, how much more so ordinary humans? Or, if one desires to summon [someone], then having drawn the *yantra* on a skull, one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood.
He by whose name [this is performed] arrives at that very moment with the speed of the wind.

If the practitioner, desiring to make someone insane, takes the fruit of the *dhuttūra* plant, mixes it with human flesh and the powder of woodworms, and gives it to someone in their food or drink while reciting the mantra, that person becomes insane at that very moment.
After seven days, he dies. Now, there is another application.

Having written the Yamāri mantra on a cloth from a cremation ground using substances such as poison and the like, and having fashioned an image together with Vairocana using a great lamp, one should place the mantra within its heart. Then, having gone to a cemetery and cut [the image] with a sharp weapon upon a funeral pyre fire, the practitioner, standing in the *vikṛtānana* (distorted-face) yoga, should anoint the body with Vairocana and offer it as an oblation facing south; [the victim] dies instantly, [driven] by the force of the wind.
The fruit of the *dhuttūra* plant; [the text reads] *dhūrapha* in BPC, *dhūturaphela* in A, *dhurapha* in Bac, and *ghuṇacūrṇena* (with the powder of woodworms);

[one should] recite [the mantra]; [the text reads] *(ja)peta* in BPC, with *pet* deleted in Bac; within seven days; [the text reads] *saptāhena* in B, *satpāheṇa* in A, and *saptāhe* in Bac; he dies; [the text reads] *mriyate* in A and BPC, and *miyate* in Bac; furthermore; [the text reads] *athāparaḥ* in A, and *athāpara* in B; the application; [the text reads] *prayogaḥ* in BPC, and *prayoga* in A and Bac; by means of poisons and the like; [the text reads] *viṣādibhiḥ* in B, and *viṣādibhi* in A; of him; [the text reads] *tasya* in B, and *yasya* in A and Sed.
In the heart; having cut [it] and remained in the application of a distorted face; by means of Vairocana, one should offer the oblation; he dies.
Alternatively, there is the application for causing enmity:

having taken the bones of a crow and an owl, one should write the ten-syllable mantra with an iron thorn together with the name of the person to be affected. Standing in a secluded place, one should recite it; he whose name was used will become hostile. [Then] regarding the wheel of Yama: having written the names of a man and a woman on birch bark, one should place them inside the belly of a frog and set it beneath a threshold; the body of whichever person’s name was used will be pierced by weapons.
Now follows the ritual application for paralyzing a maiden:
having drawn the Yamāri yantra on a cemetery cloth with poison and other substances, one should fashion a deformed effigy one span in length using charcoal from a funeral pyre;
then, having placed [the yantra] within its heart, one should set it up.
Pressing the yantra with the left foot in the form of a buffalo-faced yoga, one should mutter the ten-syllable mantra, "I quickly paralyze such-and-such a girl"; she is paralyzed.
These rites must not be told to anyone;
if a practitioner performs them out of delusion, he falls into a fierce hell.

One should perform [the rite] against one who harms the Three Jewels or one who betrays the guru; he falls into [hell]. With an iron thorn from those two, one should mutter [the mantra] over the names of the man and woman who are hostile [to him]. *asthi* (A); *asthim* (B); *tayor lohakaṇṭakena* (Sed.); *tayorohakaṇṭakena* (A); *tayorahikaṇṭakena* (B); *tayorahi kaṇṭakena* (rec.); *japeta* (A); *japata* (B); *yasya* (A); *ya* (B); *vidviṣṭo* (A, B, Sed.); *viddho* (rec.); *strīpumsayor* (B); *strīpumsaso* (A); *nāmanī* (omitted in all mss.); *nāma* (Sed.).

Having written [it]; having written it on A; having written it on BPC, Sed.; having written it on Bac; in the belly of a frog; B; in the belly of a *durdura* [frog], A; pierced by weapons; B; pierced by weapons, A; the *yamāri*-yantra; the *yamāma*-mantra, BPC, Sed.; the *yamāli*-yantra, A; the *yamāma*-mantra, Bac; on a cloth from a cremation ground; on a cloth trembling in a cremation ground, A, B; not having written; B; having engraved, A; measuring one *vitasti*; measuring a *vitrasti*, A; measuring a *vitrastī*, Bac; measuring a *vitrasti*, BPC; one should have made; one should make, BPC; one should cause to be made, A; one should make, Bac; omits "quickly"; quickly, A, B; "I paralyze," A, B, Sed.; "one should paralyze," A, B, Sed.; of deluded nature, A; of great nature, B; in a fierce hell, B; in a cruel hell, A; for those who harm the Three Jewels, A, B; for those who harm the Three Jewels, Sed.
It must be done; [it is] to be performed.

For one who has fallen away from the rules of the covenant, who mocks the mantra-tantras, and who harms sentient beings—the practitioner of mantras, having taken up their welfare with a mind moistened by compassion, performs the application of the mantras.

If [one] does so, it is stated elsewhere: "Those men who are intent on reviling the Teacher and who disparage the Mahāyāna, and who treat with derision those who know the application of mantra and tantra, should be killed with effort, or else their place should be moved. Otherwise, if a merciless yogin performs [this rite] against anyone at all, that karma remains fixed as his own. Why? Because the yogin causes harm to sentient beings.

Thus ends the second chapter, on the accomplishment of all activities, in the *Śrī-Mañjuśrī-nāma-mahāvajrabhairava-yoga-tantra*. For those who have violated their commitments (*samaya*), those who mock the mantra-tantras, and those who harm sentient beings—for them, through compassion, the mantras shall result in the Great Raurava hell. [Regarding] those who break their commitments, [the following applies]. Furthermore, for one who knows the application of the mantra-tantras, there is the *Pratyaṅgirā* and the third chapter, the *Mantroddhāraṇa-kalpa*. Now, I shall explain the extraction of the mantras (*mantroddhāraṇa*) correctly and in due order.
Standing in a pure place, the mantra-practitioner should extract the mantra:
the first of the sixth [group], the fifth of the fifth, the second of the sixth joined with the second vowel.
(1) The third of the second [group], joined again with the second vowel; and the third of the fourth, [joined with] the third.
(2) The fifth of the fifth, joined with the thirteenth vowel; the first of the sixth, doubled, joined with the eleventh vowel.
(3) The fifth of the fifth, traversed by the eleventh vowel; the third of the fourth, traversed by the thirteenth vowel.

(4) The second letter of the sixth [group], joined with the fifth vowel; the fifth of the third [group]; then one should place the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Y), joined with the thirteenth vowel (Ū). (5) The third of the fourth [group]; then the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Y); then the first of the sixth [group]; the third of the fourth [group]. (6) Then again the seed-syllable of Vāyu (Y), joined with the thirteenth vowel (Ū); the fifth of the fourth [group], joined with the third vowel (I). (7)
Then one should give the seed-syllable of fire, and likewise the seed-syllable of wind; then one should give the final letter of the alphabet conjoined with the eleventh vowel.
(8) The first of the sixth [group] shall then be the seed-syllable of wind; then one should give the final letter of the alphabet conjoined with the eleventh vowel.
Then one should give the seed-syllable of wind. (9)
One should cause that first [syllable] of the second [group] to be doubled;
(10) the fifth [syllable] of the fourth [group], joined with the third vowel, and then one should place the seed-syllable of fire joined with the second vowel. (11)
One should then give the fifth seed-syllable of the fifth [vowel], namely *va*,
joined with Vairocana (*dyam*) and the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
[Then] the second of the fifth and the first of the third.
The wise one should cause it to be recited twice.

This is the root mantra of Mahiṣamukha from the *Mañjuśrī-nāma-mahāvajrabhairava-tantra*. Through a hundred thousand recitations, this king of mantras performs all rites; such a one has never existed before, nor will there ever be again.
This performs all ritual actions;
it is the fourth [syllable] of the seventh [vowel-group], joined with the fourth vowel.
Then the All-pervading Lord should place the seed-syllable of fire, ending in the sixteenth [vowel]. (14)

one should assign Vairocana as the first.

In the *Mañjuśrī-ākhya-mahāvajrabhairava-tantra*, this is the king of mantras, the root mantra that performs all activities (*sarvakarmakara*). The wise one should place [the syllable] *na* as the fourth, conjoined with the fourth vowel. Below it, he should place [the syllable] resembling fire (*ra*). This is the mantra that performs all activities. Then, the second [syllable], conjoined with the second vowel, ending with the fifth [vowel]—that which is at the end of the fifth—is to be placed at the conclusion of the recollection, having been fully mounted upon emptiness itself. (22ab)

The second [syllable] of the fifth and the first of the third—this is proclaimed as the heart-mantra of Mahiṣamukha. By reciting it one hundred thousand times, one who is well-composed and engaged in the ritual procedure for extracting the mantra accomplishes whatever tasks exist within the three realms.

Thus ends the third chapter, the Ritual for Extracting the Mantra, in the *Śrī-Mañjuśrī-nāma-mahāvajrabhairava-yoga-tantra*. At its conclusion: *samākrāntam* (emended; Acri; *tathāntake* B; *tratthāntake* A). [The passage from *smaraṇam* to *samākrāntam* is omitted in Ts and Sed. Whatever activities exist within the three realms—these are to be performed here at this time of the ritual for extracting the mantras (mantroddhāraṇavidhi). Thus ends the third chapter, the section on the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāraṇakalpa). Now, I shall fully explain the *sādhana* of Vajrabhairava, which is the fourth chapter, the section on meditation (dhyānakalpa).
One should first take as the object of focus the deity, preceded by the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*).
First, one should recite the mantra:

"I am pure by nature, having the intrinsic nature of the selflessness of all phenomena" (*svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*). Having done so, one should contemplate that within the center of space, a wind mandala has arisen from the syllable *YAM*, appearing in the form of the color of smoke.

Having visualized a moon disc arising from the first vowel [A] above that, and having produced Mañjuśrī as a youth by means of the syllable *DHIḤ* above that, one should meditate on a sun disc produced from the syllable *ĀḤ* in his heart.

From that sun disc, a web of light rays issues forth, inciting the Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, knowledge-deities, wrathful deities, and so forth, who reside throughout the infinite and boundless ten directions.

Having returned to that [place], I shall now thoroughly explain [the practice] preceded by the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmyapūrvakam*). First, thinking "I am pure by nature" (*svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*), one should visualize a moon mandala produced from the first vowel (*ādyasvarasambhūtam*) in the center of the sky (*khamadhye*). *Punar āgatya tasmin athātaḥ sampravakṣyāmi sarvadharmanairātmyapūrvakam | prathamam svabhāvaśuddho ’ham iti khamadhye nispannam dhūmavarṇakārām ādyasvarasambhūtam candramaṇḍalam vicintya ||* [Note: The textual variants provided indicate that the Tibetan translations (Ts, Tś, etc. generally support the emendations *sampravakṣyāmi*, *sarvadharmanairātmyapūrvakam*, *svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*, *khamadhye*, *nispannam*, *dhūmavarṇakārām*, *ādyasvarasambhūtam*, and *candramaṇḍalam* as found in the critical edition.]

Having emanated [them], having performed worship according to the ritual rules,
[one visualizes] the Bodhisattvas who abide throughout the infinite and boundless [realms].
One should visualize [the] Vidyādevis entering into the solar disc.
One should contemplate that solar disc as having become one with Mañjuśrī and those Tathāgatas and others.
One should meditate on a form blazing with light, extending for a hundred thousand *yojanas*. Above that, one should visualize the syllable *HŪṂ* of black color, endowed with five rays of light.
Then, having emitted rays from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should perform the withdrawal according to the previously mentioned procedure until its conclusion.

One should visualize Vajrabhairava with nine faces, the form of a buffalo, sixteen feet, and thirty-four arms; naked, black in color, and of great splendor; his crest adorned with skulls, extremely terrifying, with an erect linga, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, with a large belly and massive body, hair standing on end, and a blazing, radiant appearance; roaring like the time of the great dissolution, devouring human blood, fat, marrow, flesh, and bone-marrow, and swallowing the three worlds including Brahmā, Upendra, Rudra, and the others.
Laughing with a loud laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*) and having a lolling tongue, he is the terror even of terror itself.

First is the buffalo face; on the right horn are three faces—blue, red, and yellow—with angry, wide-open mouths; on the left are white, smoky-grey, and black. Between those two is a deep red face with blood dripping from its throat. Above that is the face of Mañjuśrī, very yellow, slightly wrathful, adorned with youthful ornaments, five locks of hair, and a crest. He is a youth.
Having thus made [the visualization] firm, the practitioner, well-composed, should meditate.
Having emitted the syllable *hūṃ* endowed with five rays of light, and having withdrawn it according to the previously mentioned procedure, he should [visualize] the syllable *hūṃ*.

[Then, he should visualize] Mañjuśrī’s face: with a large belly, a radiant form, possessing fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone; together with Brahmā, Upendra, and others; with blood flowing from his throat; with a very yellow face; slightly wrathful; adorned with the ornaments of a youth, the five locks of hair, and a crown; a prince—having thus made [the visualization] firm, the practitioner, well-composed, should meditate.

Then, on the first right arm is a small knife (*kaṭṭārikā*), on the second a slingshot (*bhiṇḍipāla*), on the third a pestle (*musala*), on the fourth a razor (*cchurikā*), on the fifth a mallet (*kaṇapa*), on the sixth an axe (*kuṭhāra*), on the seventh a spear (*kunta*), on the eighth an arrow (*śara*), on the ninth a hook (*aṅkuśa*), on the tenth a mace (*gadā*), on the eleventh a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), on the twelfth a wheel (*cakra*), on the thirteenth a thunderbolt (*vajra*), on the fourteenth a thunderbolt-mallet (*vajramudgara*), on the fifteenth a sword (*khadga*), and on the sixteenth a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*).

In the left hands: in the first, a skull-cup; in the second, a head; in the third, a shield; in the fourth, a foot; in the fifth, a noose; in the sixth, a bow; in the seventh, an intestine; in the eighth, a bell; in the ninth, a hand; in the tenth, a cloth from a cremation ground; in the eleventh, a man pierced by a trident; in the twelfth, a fire-pit; in the thirteenth, a drinking vessel; in the fourteenth, a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*); in the fifteenth, a triple-bannered gesture (*tripatākā*); in the sixteenth, a wind-cloth; and with two [hands], he holds an elephant-hide. At his right feet are a man, a buffalo, a bull, a donkey, a camel, a dog, a deer, a ram, and a jackal.
On the left foot are the vulture, owl, crow, parrot, hawk, great mantra-reciter, great omen-bird, and crane.
One should have such a meditation on Vajrabhairava painted in this manner.
[Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Ritual of Meditation, in the *Śrī-Mahāvajrabhairavayogatantra* known as Mañjuśrī.]

The knife, the *bhiṇḍipāla* (javelin), the pestle, the small dagger, the *kaṇapa* (bludgeon), the axe, the spear, the arrow, the goad, the *khaṭvāṅga*, and as the thirteenth, the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and the thunderbolt-mallet; [at the fifteenth] the sword, the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), the skull, the shield, the deer, the parrot, and the hawk—thus says the Great Mantrin.
This concludes the fourth chapter, the "Ritual of Meditation," in the *Śrī-Mahāvajrabhairava-tantra* known as Mañjuśrī.
The fifth chapter is the "Ritual of the Cloth Painting" (*paṭavidhāna*).
One who is pure in soul, youthful, steadfast, free from craving, free from conceptual construction, not deceitful, free from anger, highly skilled, dexterous, faithful, and compassionate—
such a person becomes a painter. Alternatively, one may have it painted by an initiate (samayin) who is also a painter.
The supreme practitioner should draw [the mandala] upon a hero’s rag, or a rag covered with a corpse, or a rag from a birth, or a rag stained with great blood, or rags adorned with women’s flowers.

Regarding this, the procedure is as follows: standing in a secret place, one should have it drawn by one who is well-composed, using the five pigments as prescribed, which have been processed with resin, camphor, and so forth, and which are obtained from those residing in hell.
The practitioner should write [the mantra] with a needle on the hair of a corpse and must not show it to others. And the painter shall depict [the deity] on a cloth:

sixteen-footed, thirty-four-armed, nine-faced, naked, black in color, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, extremely terrifying, the terror even of fear itself, with the sexual organ erect. One should paint him thus on the cloth.

First is the buffalo face; on the right horn are three faces—blue, red, and yellow—with angry, wide-open mouths; on the left are white, smoky-grey, and black. Between those two, one should draw a deep red [face]. Above that, one should have drawn the face of Mañjuśrī, yellow and slightly wrathful.

In his own right hand [he holds] a small knife (kaṭṭārikā), a slingshot (bhiṇḍipāla), a club (muṣala), a razor (kṣurikā), and a skull-topped mace (kaṇapa). Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) as shown by the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava:
[the practitioner] should be pure in soul (śuddhātman), free from craving (vitṛṣṇa), and dark-complexioned (syāma).
Free from thirst for [sensual] objects (vātṛṣṇaḥ); free from malice (akrodhaḥ); not wrathful (akrodhanaḥ); compassionate (dayāluḥ);
one who abides by the commitments (samayī).

holding a damaru and a khaṭvāṅga, with his crest-jewel decorated by a skull-cup, laughing, and entering that cremation ground; having placed this painting in a secluded spot, one should offer incense of mahāmāṃsa.

In front of him, the mantra-practitioner, being well-composed, should recite the mantra three times a day using a large conch-shell rosary; he must guard it with great effort and never place it within the reach of anyone else.
One should not display before anyone linctuses,
drinks, foods, edibles, or great meats, and so forth, [whether they be] yakṣas or vetālas.

[It should be] endowed with [the following]: the fear of men impaled on stakes and so forth. One should depict there a man impaled on a stake, being burned, and suspended from a *vāṭa*-tree. One should draw [him] laughing, entering the cremation ground with a crest [on his head]. Having done this, the mantra-practitioner must protect the cloth at the three times of day. He should never give it to anyone else to eat, drink, or consume; rather, he should always eat [from it] at night.
"Three times a day, incense should be offered before the cloth painting with blood from Vairocana, if one desires the supreme accomplishment.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Ritual for the Cloth Painting, in the *Śrī-Mahāvajrabhairava-yogatantra* known as the *Mañjuśrī*. Incense should be offered three times a day in the *Yogatantra*, the Ritual for the Cloth Painting.
Now, therefore, the ritual for the fire oblation (*homa*). The sixth chapter, the Ritual for the Fire Oblation, I shall explain in due order and according to the rules.

First of all, the practitioner, having gone to a cremation ground at night, should commence the rite of *homa*. Remaining in the previously mentioned deity-yoga, he performs all the rites; then, all [the materials], namely human bone, *vairocana*, and donkey [bone], are gathered together in one place. In this regard, the ritual is as follows:
When one desires to kill [an enemy], one should collect earth, thorns, hair, and nails;

having thoroughly mixed all of that with oil, one should, with a concentrated mind, facing south, offer oblations one hundred and eight times into a funeral pyre fire while reciting the name of the person. Within three days, that person will die.
If not, then standing in a secluded place and having prepared a triangular fire-pit, one should offer oblations into a *caṇḍāla* fire using those same aforementioned substances.
By that very yoga, he is led to the realm of Death; of this there is no doubt.

Alternatively, having prepared crow’s flesh together with camel meat mixed with liquor, one should offer it into the sacrificial fire while reciting the name of the person [to be targeted]; at that moment, one causes them to be driven away.
[The practitioner should be] naked, with hair disheveled, and [the victim becomes] like a thorn, itching, and subdued.

Alternatively, one desiring to bring someone under control should visualize a red form and, facing west, offer oblations with black sesame seeds mixed with red flower-essence and adamantine water (vajrodaka) while reciting the name of the person; within seven days, he brings that person under control, and for as long as they live, he does not let them go.
These rites must be performed by one who has completed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*);
otherwise, there is no doubt that he will become an object of ridicule for all the world.
One must not disclose this to anyone.
If there is disclosure, a person attains neither accomplishment nor happiness.
Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should not reveal this range of ritual activity before anyone.
If one wishes to perform it there, it should be performed alone.
Then all the rites of the ministers will be accomplished.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Ritual Procedure for Fire Offering (Homa), in the *Śrīmahāvajrabhairavayogatantra* known as Mañjuśrī.]

By the minister; Em. minister K, R.
This minister should be appointed;
this one must not be spoken to.
The expansion [of the teaching] is to be told.
Now, the application of meditation for reviving one bitten by a venomous snake is described: the golden wind-maṇḍala empowered by the syllable *YAM* is taught.
Having visualized an eight-petaled lotus of white color in one’s own heart, one should contemplate upon it the third vowel (*Ī*) and, upon its eight petals, the eight white-colored syllables *PHAṬ*.
And by means of this [mantra], one should visualize oneself in the form of the Naga Śeṣa, white in color. On his head, one should visualize the syllable *I* dripping with nectar (*amṛta*).
One should then visualize nectar issuing forth from the eyes of that Naga and falling upon the body of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
By means of this yoga of meditation, one renders the poison that pervades the three realms into a state free of poison.
One may even consume poison a thousand times over.
Now follows the application of the meditation on liquefaction (*drāvaṇadhyāna*).
Having visualized the person to be accomplished (sādhya) before oneself, one should contemplate at his feet a bow-shaped [wind mandala] of smoky color.
Above that, in the secret region, one should contemplate a triangular fire mandala presided over by the syllable *repha* (*ra*).
Above that, one should contemplate a yellow, square earth mandala presided over by the syllable *laṃ*.
Above that, having visualized a moon disc upon the forehead,
one should contemplate within its center the syllable *VĀṂ*, from which nectar flows downward. Having thus visualized it well, one should kindle the fire with the wind.
One should contemplate that the Maheśvara-maṇḍala is being heated by that fire.

One should visualize that Mahendra-maṇḍala as being heated by fire; that nectar-maṇḍala as melting, and oneself as white in color. One should contemplate the nectar flowing from the syllable *I* upon one's head, issuing forth as nectar from the eyes of that Nāga and falling upon his body. [One should contemplate] the poison filling the three realms, [and] the smoke-colored poison [at] the feet. At the secret place, there is a moon-maṇḍala with the syllable *VAM*; by means of that fire, one should contemplate that Mahendra-maṇḍala being heated. It causes a woman to melt like a milky tree.
Then, one who desires to bring under control the king and the royal minister should, by means of the buffalo-faced yoga, remain [in that state] and meditate upon oneself as being red in color.
One should enter into the midst of where the person to be accomplished (sādhya) resides;
thereafter, one should project from one's own body a form holding a goad and a noose in its hands.
He sees Mañjuśrī being brought to the heart and throat of the person to be converted (sādhya).
He should cause Mañjuśrī to enter [the sādhya].
Having caused him to enter the body of Mañjuśrī, he should visualize that Mañjuśrī, having become red in color, has bound that sādhya and rendered him utterly distressed.
By means of this practice of meditative concentration, one should contemplate the ten-syllable mantra, red in color, within his heart.

Furthermore, by this very yoga, the practitioner causes a woman to melt [subjugate her]. By means of the *kṣīrin* tree, a royal minister; by means of a minister, a buffalo. Through the yoga of the buffalo-faced one, the practitioner should enter wherever the target resides; he should enter into the midst of that place. With hook and noose in hand (*aṅkuśapāśahasta*), red in color, in the form of Mañjuśrī—having bound the target at the heart and throat with Mañjuśrī, he beholds Mañjuśrī. Having caused him to enter the body of Mañjuśrī, he should contemplate that target as being rendered utterly overwhelmed. By this application of meditation, he should visualize the ten-syllable mantra, red in color, within the heart.

Furthermore, the practitioner, in the form of gnosis (*jñāna*), should enter into those syllables. He should contemplate the object to be accomplished as having become one with them through this application of meditation; by means of this, he brings [the deity] under control for as long as he lives, without doubt, even a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) within seven days. This tantra must be performed by a mantra-reciter who is stable in meditation and well-composed.
The mantra must never be given to anyone at any time;
the meditation on the yoga of the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava must not be given to anyone nor spoken of;
the mantra must not be disclosed.
One should not display the cloth before anyone;
the cloth must be kept secret. One should not recite the application of this mantra in the presence of anyone, nor should one perform the fire offering (homa).

If one should say: "By the command of the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava, the ḍākinīs or the yoginīs shall devour those who violate the *samaya*," therefore, the mantra-practitioner must not give [the mantra] to anyone.

Or rather, it may be given to one who does not break the *samaya*, who is free from conceptual construction, firm in his vows, devoted to the guru, disciplined, solely intent upon the teaching of the Tathāgata, a keeper of secret mantras, free from anger, compassionate, dedicated to recitation and meditation, and fearless.

To such a disciple, distinguished by these qualities, who has beheld the maṇḍala, one should contemplate the object to be accomplished through this application. Within seven days, even a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) will be brought under control; for as long as one lives, there is no doubt. Through stable meditation, the tantra should be given to someone, and at times a mantra; to someone else, meditation should be imparted. One should extend the application by the command of Vajrabhairava and the yoginīs. To one who betrays the pledge (*samaya*), it must not be given. It should be given to a disciple who does not violate the pledge, who is firm in his vows, who is solely devoted to the teaching of the Tathāgata, who keeps his mantra secret, and who is intent upon recitation and meditation—to such a disciple who possesses these qualities, who has deep devotion toward the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava, whose mind is moistened with great compassion, who is free from conceptual construction, who is devoted to the guru, and whose virtues have been thoroughly examined. To that disciple, the *Śrīmahāvajrabhairavatantra* should be bestowed.
There is no doubt that in this world one experiences great terror; because of violating the samaya, one goes to hell, one shall go to hell.

In this *Paraloka-mañjuśrīyākhyamahāvajrabhairavacakrayogatantro*, the seventh chapter, the *Kalpa on the Examination of the Accomplishment of Meditative Action*, is concluded. This is a portion of the ritual manual extracted from the tantra concerning the characteristics of the wheel of the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava, originating from the glorious seat (*pīṭha*) of Oḍḍiyāna; it is accomplished through recitation. Here ends the ritual manual for the accomplishment of the siddhi of the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava with the face of a buffalo. By this merit, may the world become equal to the glorious Mahāvajrabhairava! OM HRIH STRIḤ VIKṚTĀNANA HŪM PHAṬ. OM YAMĀNTAKA HŪM PHAṬ.

To a disciple who possesses firm devotion, whose mind is moistened by great compassion, who is free from conceptual construction, who is devoted to the guru, and whose qualities have been thoroughly examined—the disciple proceeds toward great fear and experiences [suffering] in the next world due to having violated the *samaya*. This concludes the chapter on examination in this *Mañjuśrīyākhyamahāvajrabhairavacakrayogatantra*.
